body:
We like to imagine the brain as a hard drive: you save
something once, and it's there when you need it.

It doesn't work like that. Every time we recall something,
the brain rebuilds it from past experience, associations, context, and how
recently and how often we've used it.

Think of a student preparing for an exam. They studied the
subject months ago, and the knowledge is probably still in there somewhere. But
on exam day, it's stubborn about showing up.

Then revision starts. They solve problems, recall concepts,
get things wrong, and fix them. Slowly, everything becomes easier to pull out.

Why? Because the learning was brought back to life and
strengthened by actually using it.

Professional competence works the same way.

A small detour into machine learning

Machine learning systems get better by seeing lots of data
and picking out patterns. The more relevant and well-organised the data, the
better the output.

People are obviously not machines. Still, the parallel is
hard to ignore: repeated exposure, practice and feedback shape performance.

There's a catch, too. Feed a system poor data and it learns
the wrong pattern. People do the same. If an employee keeps doing a task
incorrectly and nobody steps in, the mistake quietly turns into a habit.

So repeating training isn't enough. We have to repeat the *right*
behaviour.

Training is not competence

Here's where many organisations get stuck.

Someone attends a programme, passes the assessment, collects
the certificate, and the training record gets closed. Done.

But has any competence actually been built? Not necessarily.

Training gives people knowledge. Competence is the
ability to apply that knowledge properly and consistently in real situations.

Take leadership. Someone can sit through a two-day programme
and come away understanding delegation, communication, motivation, conflict and
decision-making. Then real life arrives:

That's where competence shows itself. Not in the training
room, but under real conditions.

From knowledge to competence

I see this as a continuous journey:

Awareness → Knowledge → Practice → Feedback → Correction
→ Application → Competence

Training covers only a slice of it. The organisation has to
give people chances to use what they've learned, such as:

The goal isn't to get people to remember more. It's to make
the right behaviour easier to recall and show at the moment it's needed.

The trouble with training and then silence

Imagine teaching someone an emergency response procedure and
then never mentioning it again until the day an emergency happens. Would you
call that competence? Probably not.

Yet plenty of organisations work this way. Training at
induction, a mandatory refresher once a year, attendance sheets filed, and the
box is ticked.

But human performance doesn't follow the training calendar.
Competence needs reinforcing all year round, especially in high-risk industries
where one person's judgement can have serious consequences.

Leadership is built the same way

You can't create a leader by passing theories from a trainer
to a participant. Young professionals need to practise leading.

Hand them responsibility for a project. Let them lead a
small team. Ask them to sort out a conflict. Let them make decisions, and even
fail safely. Give them feedback. Then give them another go.

That's how leadership competence grows. And the same goes
for communication, safety behaviour, problem solving, decision-making, teamwork
and technical skill.

Experience only becomes valuable when we reflect on it and
turn it into learning.

So what should we measure?

Maybe it's time to stop asking only, "How many people
have we trained?"

and start asking, "What changed because we trained
them?"

Did behaviour change? Did performance improve? Can people
actually apply what they learned? Are decisions getting better? Are mistakes
being prevented? Can people respond well when circumstances shift? Are
supervisors showing the behaviours we expect from leaders?

These questions move us from training management to
competence management.

The leader's part in all this

A training department can offer learning opportunities. The
workplace decides whether that learning turns into competence.

A supervisor who encourages the right behaviour reinforces
learning. A manager who ignores poor behaviour reinforces the wrong lesson. A
leader who asks questions, gives feedback and encourages reflection keeps the
learning going.

So competence doesn't belong to the training department.
It's a leadership responsibility.

My perspective

I've worked across maritime, production and service
industries, and I've come to believe that the biggest gap in most organisations
isn't a lack of knowledge. It's the gap between what people know and
what people consistently do.

That's where human behaviour, competence management and
leadership meet.

Organisations pour money into procedures, systems,
technology and training. But in the end, systems perform through people. An
organisation's real strength isn't what's written in its procedures or how many
certificates are framed on the wall. It's whether its people understand,
practise, apply and consistently show the behaviours that success requires.

The real question

Next time you plan a training programme, try swapping the
usual question.

Not "What should we teach them?"

But "What do we want them to do differently afterwards,
and how will we help them practise until it becomes competence?"

Because training creates an opportunity to learn. Practice
builds capability. Feedback drives improvement. And consistent application
creates competence.

That's when training stops being a cost and becomes a real
business investment.

Train the mind. Practise the behaviour. Build
the competence. Improve the performance.
summary:
Want people to perform differently? Don't just train them differently. Help them practise differently.
We like to imagine the brain as a hard drive: you save something once, and it's there when you need it.
It doesn't work like that. Every time we recall something, the brain rebuilds it from past experience, associations, context, and how recently and how often we've used it.
Think of a student preparing for an exam. They studied the subject months ago, and the knowledge is probably still in there somewhere. But on exam day, it's stubborn about showing up.
author: Dr. Sundar Subramani
title: Training Doesn't Create Competence. Practice Does.
